name: Sam Cooke
hook: A gospel star who crossed over to pop, owned his own label and publishing at a time when almost no Black artist did, and wrote 'A Change Is Gonna Come' after hearing Bob Dylan.
blurb: Sam Cooke was born Samuel Cook in Clarksdale, Mississippi, on 22 January 1931, the son of a Baptist minister, and grew up in Chicago. In 1950, at 19, he replaced R. H. Harris as lead singer of the Soul Stirrers, a famous gospel group, and was a gospel star in his early twenties. In 1956 he left gospel to sing pop, which many church people thought was wrong. Art Rupe of Specialty wanted him to sound like Little Richard, so he went to Keen, where his first pop single, 'You Send Me' (1957), went to number one. He signed to RCA Victor in 1960 for a $100,000 advance, and with J. W. Alexander he started his own record label, SAR, and his own publishing and management company, Kags, so that he owned his songs and ran his own business, which very few Black musicians could do then. In 1963 he heard Bob Dylan's 'Blowin' in the Wind'. He was moved that a white writer had written such a song about American racism, and ashamed he had not written one himself. On 8 October 1963 a whites-only Holiday Inn in Shreveport, Louisiana, turned him away, and shortly after he wrote 'A Change Is Gonna Come', recorded on 30 January 1964. On 11 December 1964 he was shot dead by the manager of the Hacienda Motel in Los Angeles, Bertha Franklin. She said it was self-defence, and a coroner's jury called it justifiable homicide. His family has always questioned what happened.
